title: Your Unlearning Gives You Away: Identifying Erased Concepts in Diffusion Models

paper.title: Your Unlearning Gives You Away: Identifying Erased Concepts in Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Existing attacks on unlearned diffusion models assume that the erased concepts are known in advance and focus on recovering them. In practice, however, model providers may not disclose which concepts have been removed, and even with access to the original base model, an adversary may still lack a clear target to attack. In this paper, we aim to answer the following critical but overlooked questions: which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To this end, we present Tracer , a framework that rapidly and accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number. Tracer efficiently identifies erased concepts without generating and classifying images. By combining lightweight spectral analysis of weight footprints, it enables efficient search over large candidate vocabularies.
To distinguish multiple erased concepts, we introduce a footprint coverage objective that guides sequential discovery. Tracer estimates the number of erased concepts by detecting a sharp decline in candidate confidence as the selected concepts account for the erasure footprint, without requiring labeled examples for calibration. The framework requires only lightweight linear algebra and limited forward probes, with no prior knowledge of the unlearning algorithm.
Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods demonstrate that Tracer identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds , achieving 𝟏𝟓𝟎 \bm{150} – 137,000 × \bm{137{,}000\times} and 𝟏𝟑𝟑 \bm{133} – 20,000 × \bm{20{,}000\times} speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively, with substantially higher identification accuracy.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) exhibit powerful generative capabilities. Despite these advances, their large-scale deployment has raised concerns about copyright infringement and harmful or biased content generation. Concept unlearning ( Bourtoule et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) aims to suppress designated concepts while preserving other generative capabilities. Most existing methods achieve this by modifying pretrained model weights, demonstrating promising results in unlearning individual concepts or sets of concepts. Existing attacks exploit vulnerabilities in unlearned models to regenerate erased content, but they typically assume prior knowledge of the specific concepts to recover ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Pham et al., 2023 ; Rusanovsky et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Chin et al., 2023 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Petsiuk and Saenko, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ; Horwitz et al., 2024 ) . In practice, model providers may not disclose what they have removed. Even access to the original base model does not directly reveal which of its many concepts the provider chose to erase. For example, a provider may erase a small set of individuals’ identities for privacy reasons. Although the base model may still generate depictions of these individuals, access to this capability alone does not tell an adversary who was selected for protection. Identifying the erased concepts therefore provides information beyond access to the original model: it reveals the provider’s undisclosed targets and allows an adversary to focus subsequent attacks on the content the provider sought to suppress. This raises two critical but overlooked questions: without any prior knowledge of the erasure targets, can an adversary know which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To the best of our knowledge, no existing method systematically addresses this identification problem in unlearned diffusion models. Figure 1: (a) Motivation: existing unlearning attacks assume known unlearning targets, leaving the identification of targets unexplored. (b) Current problem: adapted MIA and brute-force method incur high computational costs and struggle to determine target counts and distinguish targets from affected non-targets. (c) Tracer : identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds without prior target knowledge, knowledge of the unlearning algorithm, or image generation. Potential approaches include adapting traditional membership inference attacks (MIAs) ( Fu et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) or comparing images generated by the original and unlearned models for each candidate. However, extending these approaches to reliable and efficient identification of unknown erasure targets presents challenges. First , unlearning can affect both target and non-target concepts. Changes in membership scores or generated content therefore cannot reliably distinguish directly targeted concepts from indirectly affected ones. Second , the number of erased concepts is unknown. Identifying the target set requires determining which candidates to select and when to stop, without target labels for calibration. Third , both approaches incur substantial computational costs even with a predefined candidate set. Without a narrowly specified set, the search may span a vocabulary containing tens of thousands of words, making repeated generation or MIA-based probing prohibitively expensive. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, Tra cing C oncepts Er ased by Unlearning ( Tracer ), for rapidly and accurately identifying erased concepts and estimates their number without any prior knowledge of the erasure targets. An intuitive but inconclusive approach is to compare the unlearned model weights with its original base model. However, these weight differences span distinct representation spaces, making it difficult to map them directly to erased concepts. To turn these differences into usable evidence , Tracer constructs Gram matrices from weight differences and uses a small set of probe words to identify compatible representation groups, then applies spectral reweighting to balance signals before aggregation, producing an erasure footprint for each group. These footprints provide the basis for identifying candidate concepts whose representations collectively explain the observed changes. To identify multiple erased concepts , we formulate identification as a subspace coverage problem, which measures how much of the erasure footprint a set of candidate concepts can collectively explain. Specifically, starting from an empty set, Tracer iteratively adds the candidate that best explains the remaining footprint energy, reducing redundant selections and directing the search toward other erased concepts. To estimate the number of erased concepts , we track candidate confidence throughout this coverage-based selection process. As the selected concepts account for the dominant footprint energy, a sharp decline in confidence indicates a cutoff in the selected sequence, allowing us to estimate the erased-set size without labeled calibration data. We summarize our contributions as follows: • To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically study erasure-target identification in unlearned diffusion models, exposing an overlooked vulnerability in diffusion unlearning. • We propose Tracer , an efficient framework that accurately identifies multiple erased concepts from large candidate vocabularies without generating or classifying images, making broad searches for undisclosed erasure targets practical. • Tracer automatically estimates how many concepts were erased, without labeled calibration examples, knowledge of the unlearning algorithm, or information about which weights were modified. • Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods show that Tracer accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number from large candidate vocabularies in seconds, achieving 𝟏𝟓𝟎 \bm{150} – 137,000 × \bm{137{,}000\times} and 𝟏𝟑𝟑 \bm{133} – 20,000 × \bm{20{,}000\times} speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.1 Concept unlearning in diffusion models.
sections.text: Fine-tuning methods steer target-concept noise toward anchor distributions ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Heng and Soh, 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Bui et al., 2025 ; Thakral et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Closed-form methods edit attention projections without retraining ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Orgad et al., 2023 ; Basu et al., 2024 ; Chavhan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026a ; Yao et al., ; Biswas et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . Inference-time methods suppress undesirable concepts via guidance or activation intervention ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Deja and others, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Recent work extends erasure to flow-matching transformers, including SD3 and FLUX ( Gao et al., 2025a ; Ranjan et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Parallel work targets text-to-video models through editing, low-rank refusal vectors, and training-free safeguards ( Liu and Tan, 2024 ; Yoon et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Facchiano et al., 2026 ) . Robust methods resist adversarial prompts and subsequent fine-tuning ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ; Bui et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Gao et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026a ) .

sections.heading: 2.2 Adversarial vulnerabilities of unlearned models.
sections.text: Recent analyses show erased concepts are often suppressed, not removed, resurfacing under subsequent benign fine-tuning or alternative sampling strategies ( Rusanovsky et al., 2025 ; Suriyakumar et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . Adversarial attacks recover erased concepts. White-box attacks exploit model gradients or internal signals ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Chin et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Pham et al., 2023 ) , whereas black-box attacks search adversarial prompts with query-only model access ( Tsai et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2025 ; Yook et al., 2025 ) . Non-prompt inference-time attacks recover concepts via concept arithmetic, image-guided inversion, or text-free inversion ( Petsiuk and Saenko, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ) , while weight-space attacks use fine-tuning or pre-erasure weights ( George et al., 2025 ; Horwitz et al., 2024 ) . Beyond unlearning attacks, diffusion models themselves also face classical privacy attacks on their original training data. Membership inference attacks determine whether a given sample actually belongs to the training set ( Matsumoto et al., 2023 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) . Data extraction and memorization attacks reconstruct or replicate individual training images from the model ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Somepalli et al., 2023b ) .

sections.heading: 2.3 Positioning of our study.
sections.text: Our study aims to identify the concepts targeted for erasure in an unlearned model. Existing attacks (Sec 2.2 ) primarily recover content associated with known erased concepts. Tracer identifies unknown erasure targets and estimates their number without image generation, fine-tuning, or knowledge of the erasure algorithm. This setting shifts the focus from attacking a model to regenerate known erased concepts to identifying which concepts were erased.

sections.heading: What the adversary holds.
sections.text: A publisher starts from public base weights W W , applies a published concept-unlearning method (Section 2.1 ) to erase an unknown set S ⋆ S^{\star} of concepts, and releases the resulting edited weights W ′ W^{\prime} . The adversary has access only to W W , W ′ W^{\prime} , and a vocabulary 𝒞 \mathcal{C} of ordinary words assumed to contain S ⋆ S^{\star} . In particular, the adversary knows neither | S ⋆ | |S^{\star}| nor which erasure algorithm was used, has no labelled examples of erased or non-erased models, and therefore cannot construct shadow models for validation. The adversary may evaluate the full computation graph on text inputs and record the inputs to all changed weight matrices, which are identified directly by comparing W W and W ′ W^{\prime} . Text-encoder matrices are probed from the prompt alone, whereas generative-backbone matrices are probed by pairing the prompt with a single fixed latent at several noise levels. Both probes require only the available model weights and architecture. The sampling loop is never executed, no image is decoded, and no model output is observed.

sections.heading: What the attack recovers.
sections.text: The goal of the attack is to recover the identities of the erased concepts: a subset S ^ ⊆ 𝒞 \hat{S}\subseteq\mathcal{C} that should coincide with S ⋆ S^{\star} , together with an inferred count n n intended to match | S ⋆ | |S^{\star}| . Because Tracer automatically searches all available aligned model matrices for weight changes and reads the representations they receive, it requires no knowledge of either the erasure algorithm or its edit locations. It therefore applies with minimal assumptions to weight-editing concept-unlearning methods across different model components and architectures.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: We evaluate Tracer on three text-to-image backbones: Stable Diffusion v1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , and FLUX.1 ( Labs, 2024 ) . The text-to-video backbones are CogVideoX-5B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) . We use official implementations and released checkpoints without modification. Object identification is evaluated on the ten Imagenette classes ( Howard and others, 2019 ) . Explicit-content evaluation uses I2P prompts ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) . Artistic-style identification covers the artists evaluated by ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) and UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) . Generation quality is evaluated on MS COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . We construct Imagenette-20 by augmenting Imagenette’s ten classes ( Howard and others, 2019 ) with 10 non-overlapping common object categories from ImageNet-1k ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) to evaluate identification across varying erased-set sizes. All experiments run on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.

sections.heading: 4.2 Disclosing Erased Concept in Unlearned Models
sections.text: Reproducing unlearning methods with their official implementations reveals limits on stable erasure capacity. Beyond these limits, models exhibit degraded forgetting or damaged generative capabilities. Shaded cells in Table 1 indicate evaluated settings within these limits; excluded settings are marked “–”. We evaluate varying erased-set sizes, where K K denotes the number of concepts jointly erased from each checkpoint. For each size, we sample concept sets from Imagenette-50, shared across methods and backbones. Each set is jointly erased to produce a checkpoint. We define recovery accuracy as the percentage of checkpoints whose recovered set exactly matches the ground-truth erased set. Correct recovery identifies all erased concepts without extras, jointly testing concept identities and inferred set size. Partial recovery counts as failure. The Avg. column averages recovery accuracy over evaluated set sizes within each method’s stable erasure range, excluding “–”. Higher values indicate better performance ( ↑ \uparrow ). Table 3 extends the same protocol to text-to-video models. Evaluation is restricted to individual concepts and small groups, where the tested methods maintain stable erasure. Tracer achieves perfect recovery for both methods on CogVideoX-5B and for Refusal on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. For VideoEraser on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, recovery remains perfect for individual concepts, with a modest decline under joint erasure. These results demonstrate that erasure footprints remain informative across video architectures with different temporal modeling, enabling accurate identification of both individual targets and jointly erased concept sets. sections.heading: 4.3 Comparison With Traditional Adversarial Methods
sections.text: We compare Tracer with two approaches. Adapted MIA ranks concepts by aggregated changes in sample-level membership scores. Brute-force probing ranks candidates by comparing images generated before and after unlearning. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.3 . We evaluate ESD, UCE, SPEED, and ScaPre on Stable Diffusion v1.5, with 50 checkpoints per erased-set size K ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 } K\in\{1,3,5\} . All approaches share checkpoints and 1,000-name vocabulary. To accommodate conventional methods, all receive the true K K ; Tracer uses its iterative selection order without size estimation. Unlike exact-set accuracy, this comparison credits partial recovery. sections.text: We evaluate components on 50 checkpoints per unlearning method at K = 5 K=5 . Table 5 provides K K to isolate concept identification from size estimation. The single imprint variant retains the imprint with the highest initial confidence in each group. Removing background suppression sets γ = 0 \gamma=0 while preserving unit normalization. Removing progressive selection uses the initial ranking without updating coverage gains, retaining lexical suppression. Tracer achieves 100% Recall@5 across four methods. Using a single imprint reduces recall by 5.2 to 16.0 percentage points, supporting evidence integration across weight changes. Removing background suppression causes declines of 7.6 to 23.2 points. Replacing progressive selection with static ranking produces the largest reduction across methods, reaching 43.6 points on ESD. These results support updating candidate scores to capture information beyond the selected span. Table 5 evaluates exact recovery of the erased set without providing K K . Replacing self-calibration with fixed parameters reduces accuracy to between 78% and 92%. Always selecting the largest confidence drop, without accounting for an initial rise, yields accuracy between 64% and 80%. The full method achieves 100% across four methods, supporting both calibration for each checkpoint and size estimation adapted to the confidence profile. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Tracer , which accurately identifies erasure targets and their number from publicly released model weights in seconds without image generation. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness across image and video backbones and diverse unlearning methods. It enables label-free search over large candidate vocabularies, achieving substantial speedups over membership inference attacks and brute-force generation-based probing methods. Our work establishes erasure-target identification as a distinct task and provides a practical and computationally efficient framework for assessing what model weights reveal about erasure targets despite suppressed generation.

Artistic-style identification covers the artists evaluated by ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) and UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) . This vocabulary covers all 1,000 ImageNet class names under case-insensitive matching and retains multiword names and capitalized proper names. sections.heading: A.2 Extension to Multiword Concept Identification
sections.text: Tracer treats each entry in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} as a complete candidate, which may contain multiple words. Identifying a multiword concept already present in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} requires no change to the main pipeline. This section describes an iterative search extension that constructs candidate phrases from individual words. The extension uses the text-aware footprint to guide expansion and selects a phrase length without knowing the target length in advance.

sections.heading: Candidate Initialization and Expansion.
sections.text: We construct a candidate word vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} from alphabetic CLIP tokenizer entries ending with </w> . Each entry contains at least two characters after removing the marker and is represented by a single token. The initial candidate set 𝒞 ( 1 ) \mathcal{C}^{(1)} contains all single-word entries in 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Candidates at expansion round j j contain exactly j j words. This construction covers phrases whose constituent words are each represented by a retained token. At round j j , we retain the b b highest-scoring candidates in a set ℬ ( j ) \mathcal{B}^{(j)} . Each retained candidate is expanded by inserting a word from 𝒱 \mathcal{V} at every possible position: 𝒞 ( j + 1 ) = { Insert ( c , v , i ) | c ∈ ℬ ( j ) , v ∈ 𝒱 , i = 0 , … , j } . \mathcal{C}^{(j+1)}=\left\{\operatorname{Insert}(c,v,i)\,\middle|\,c\in\mathcal{B}^{(j)},\ v\in\mathcal{V},\ i=0,\ldots,j\right\}. (8) Here, Insert ⁡ ( c , v , i ) \operatorname{Insert}(c,v,i) inserts v v after the first i i words of c c , including before the first word and after the last. Duplicate sequences are removed, while distinct word orders remain separate candidates. Expansion draws from the full vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , allowing words with low individual scores to contribute to a phrase.

The search may therefore return a shorter phrase even when the complete target has been generated.

sections.heading: A.3 Baseline Implementations
sections.text: We compare Tracer with brute-force generation probing and an adapted membership inference attack ( Kong et al., 2024 ) . Both baselines assign a score to each candidate c ∈ 𝒞 c\in\mathcal{C} based on changes between the public base model W W and the unlearned model W ′ W^{\prime} . Candidates are ranked in descending order of these scores.

sections.heading: Brute-Force Generation Probing.
sections.text: This baseline evaluates whether a candidate concept becomes less evident in generated images after unlearning. For each candidate c c , we construct prompts containing the complete candidate name and generate images using both W W and W ′ W^{\prime} . Let ℐ W ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{W}(c) and ℐ W ′ ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{W^{\prime}}(c) denote the corresponding image sets. We score the candidate by the decrease in average concept evidence: s BF ​ ( c ) = 1 | ℐ W ​ ( c ) | ​ ∑ I ∈ ℐ W ​ ( c ) a ⁡ ( I , c ) − 1 | ℐ W ′ ​ ( c ) | ​ ∑ I ∈ ℐ W ′ ​ ( c ) a ⁡ ( I , c ) , s_{\mathrm{BF}}(c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{W}(c)|}\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{W}(c)}a(I,c)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{W^{\prime}}(c)|}\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{W^{\prime}}(c)}a(I,c), (12) where a ⁡ ( I , c ) a(I,c) measures the evidence for concept c c in image I I . A larger score indicates a greater decline in the model’s ability to generate the candidate concept. The same evaluation function is used for both models. This procedure requires image generation for every candidate in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Changes in generated content may also reflect effects on related non-target concepts, which can receive high scores despite not being directly targeted.

sections.heading: Adapted Membership Inference Attack.
sections.text: We adapt PIA Kong et al. (2024) from sample-level membership inference to concept-level identification. For each candidate c c , let 𝒳 c \mathcal{X}_{c} denote its associated evaluation samples. We apply the PIA error statistic to the same samples under W W and W ′ W^{\prime} and aggregate the differences: s PIA ​ ( c ) = 1 | 𝒳 c | ​ ∑ x ∈ 𝒳 c [ r W ′ ​ ( x , c ) − r W ​ ( x , c ) ] , s_{\mathrm{PIA}}(c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{c}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{c}}\left[r_{W^{\prime}}(x,c)-r_{W}(x,c)\right], (13) where r W ​ ( x , c ) r_{W}(x,c) denotes the sample-level PIA error computed using model W W with concept conditioning c c . A larger score indicates a greater increase in error after unlearning. Averaging over 𝒳 c \mathcal{X}_{c} converts the sample-level changes into a single candidate score. The adaptation ranks concepts by changes in the PIA statistic rather than making binary membership decisions for individual samples. Its concept scores may capture both direct erasure effects and changes affecting non-target concepts.

In practice, however, model providers may not disclose which concepts have been removed, and even with access to the original base model, an adversary may still lack a clear target to attack. In this paper, we aim to answer the following critical but overlooked questions: which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To this end, we present Tracer , a framework that rapidly and accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number. Tracer efficiently identifies erased concepts without generating and classifying images. By combining lightweight spectral analysis of weight footprints, it enables efficient search over large candidate vocabularies. To distinguish multiple erased concepts, we introduce a footprint coverage objective that guides sequential discovery. Tracer estimates the number of erased concepts by detecting a sharp decline in candidate confidence as the selected concepts account for the erasure footprint, without requiring labeled examples for calibration. The framework requires only lightweight linear algebra and limited forward probes, with no prior knowledge of the unlearning algorithm. Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods demonstrate that Tracer identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds , achieving 𝟏𝟓𝟎 \bm{150} – 137,000 × \bm{137{,}000\times} and 𝟏𝟑𝟑 \bm{133} – 20,000 × \bm{20{,}000\times} speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively, with substantially higher identification accuracy. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) exhibit powerful generative capabilities. Despite these advances, their large-scale deployment has raised concerns about copyright infringement and harmful or biased content generation. Concept unlearning ( Bourtoule et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) aims to suppress designated concepts while preserving other generative capabilities. Most existing methods achieve this by modifying pretrained model weights, demonstrating promising results in unlearning individual concepts or sets of concepts. Existing attacks exploit vulnerabilities in unlearned models to regenerate erased content, but they typically assume prior knowledge of the specific concepts to recover ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Pham et al., 2023 ; Rusanovsky et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Chin et al., 2023 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Petsiuk and Saenko, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ; Horwitz et al., 2024 ) . In practice, model providers may not disclose what they have removed. Even access to the original base model does not directly reveal which of its many concepts the provider chose to erase. For example, a provider may erase a small set of individuals’ identities for privacy reasons. Although the base model may still generate depictions of these individuals, access to this capability alone does not tell an adversary who was selected for protection. Identifying the erased concepts therefore provides information beyond access to the original model: it reveals the provider’s undisclosed targets and allows an adversary to focus subsequent attacks on the content the provider sought to suppress. This raises two critical but overlooked questions: without any prior knowledge of the erasure targets, can an adversary know which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To the best of our knowledge, no existing method systematically addresses this identification problem in unlearned diffusion models. Figure 1: (a) Motivation: existing unlearning attacks assume known unlearning targets, leaving the identification of targets unexplored. (b) Current problem: adapted MIA and brute-force method incur high computational costs and struggle to determine target counts and distinguish targets from affected non-targets. (c) Tracer : identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds without prior target knowledge, knowledge of the unlearning algorithm, or image generation. Potential approaches include adapting traditional membership inference attacks (MIAs) ( Fu et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) or comparing images generated by the original and unlearned models for each candidate. However, extending these approaches to reliable and efficient identification of unknown erasure targets presents challenges. First , unlearning can affect both target and non-target concepts. Changes in membership scores or generated content therefore cannot reliably distinguish directly targeted concepts from indirectly affected ones. Second , the number of erased concepts is unknown. Identifying the target set requires determining which candidates to select and when to stop, without target labels for calibration. Third , both approaches incur substantial computational costs even with a predefined candidate set. Without a narrowly specified set, the search may span a vocabulary containing tens of thousands of words, making repeated generation or MIA-based probing prohibitively expensive. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, Tra cing C oncepts Er ased by Unlearning ( Tracer ), for rapidly and accurately identifying erased concepts and estimates their number without any prior knowledge of the erasure targets. An intuitive but inconclusive approach is to compare the unlearned model weights with its original base model. However, these weight differences span distinct representation spaces, making it difficult to map them directly to erased concepts. To turn these differences into usable evidence , Tracer constructs Gram matrices from weight differences and uses a small set of probe words to identify compatible representation groups, then applies spectral reweighting to balance signals before aggregation, producing an erasure footprint for each group. These footprints provide the basis for identifying candidate concepts whose representations collectively explain the observed changes. To identify multiple erased concepts , we formulate identification as a subspace coverage problem, which measures how much of the erasure footprint a set of candidate concepts can collectively explain. Specifically, starting from an empty set, Tracer iteratively adds the candidate that best explains the remaining footprint energy, reducing redundant selections and directing the search toward other erased concepts. To estimate the number of erased concepts , we track candidate confidence throughout this coverage-based selection process. As the selected concepts account for the dominant footprint energy, a sharp decline in confidence indicates a cutoff in the selected sequence, allowing us to estimate the erased-set size without labeled calibration data. We summarize our contributions as follows: • To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically study erasure-target identification in unlearned diffusion models, exposing an overlooked vulnerability in diffusion unlearning. • We propose Tracer , an efficient framework that accurately identifies multiple erased concepts from large candidate vocabularies without generating or classifying images, making broad searches for undisclosed erasure targets practical. • Tracer automatically estimates how many concepts were erased, without labeled calibration examples, knowledge of the unlearning algorithm, or information about which weights were modified. • Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods show that Tracer accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number from large candidate vocabularies in seconds, achieving 𝟏𝟓𝟎 \bm{150} – 137,000 × \bm{137{,}000\times} and 𝟏𝟑𝟑 \bm{133} – 20,000 × \bm{20{,}000\times} speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively. 2 Related Work 2.1 Concept unlearning in diffusion models. Fine-tuning methods steer target-concept noise toward anchor distributions ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Heng and Soh, 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Bui et al., 2025 ; Thakral et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Closed-form methods edit attention projections without retraining ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Orgad et al., 2023 ; Basu et al., 2024 ; Chavhan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026a ; Yao et al., ; Biswas et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . Inference-time methods suppress undesirable concepts via guidance or activation intervention ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Deja and others, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Recent work extends erasure to flow-matching transformers, including SD3 and FLUX ( Gao et al., 2025a ; Ranjan et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Parallel work targets text-to-video models through editing, low-rank refusal vectors, and training-free safeguards ( Liu and Tan, 2024 ; Yoon et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Facchiano et al., 2026 ) . Robust methods resist adversarial prompts and subsequent fine-tuning ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ; Bui et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Gao et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026a ) . 2.2 Adversarial vulnerabilities of unlearned models. Recent analyses show erased concepts are often suppressed, not removed, resurfacing under subsequent benign fine-tuning or alternative sampling strategies ( Rusanovsky et al., 2025 ; Suriyakumar et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . Adversarial attacks recover erased concepts. White-box attacks exploit model gradients or internal signals ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Chin et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Pham et al., 2023 ) , whereas black-box attacks search adversarial prompts with query-only model access ( Tsai et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2025 ; Yook et al., 2025 ) . Non-prompt inference-time attacks recover concepts via concept arithmetic, image-guided inversion, or text-free inversion ( Petsiuk and Saenko, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ) , while weight-space attacks use fine-tuning or pre-erasure weights ( George et al., 2025 ; Horwitz et al., 2024 ) . Beyond unlearning attacks, diffusion models themselves also face classical privacy attacks on their original training data. Membership inference attacks determine whether a given sample actually belongs to the training set ( Matsumoto et al., 2023 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) . Data extraction and memorization attacks reconstruct or replicate individual training images from the model ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Somepalli et al., 2023b ) . 2.3 Positioning of our study. Our study aims to identify the concepts targeted for erasure in an unlearned model. Existing attacks (Sec 2.2 ) primarily recover content associated with known erased concepts. Tracer identifies unknown erasure targets and estimates their number without image generation, fine-tuning, or knowledge of the erasure algorithm. This setting shifts the focus from attacking a model to regenerate known erased concepts to identifying which concepts were erased. 3 Method 3.1 Unlearn Threat Model What the adversary holds. A publisher starts from public base weights W W , applies a published concept-unlearning method (Section 2.1 ) to erase an unknown set S ⋆ S^{\star} of concepts, and releases the resulting edited weights W ′ W^{\prime} . The adversary has access only to W W , W ′ W^{\prime} , and a vocabulary 𝒞 \mathcal{C} of ordinary words assumed to contain S ⋆ S^{\star} . In particular, the adversary knows neither | S ⋆ | |S^{\star}| nor which erasure algorithm was used, has no labelled examples of erased or non-erased models, and therefore cannot construct shadow models for validation. The adversary may evaluate the full computation graph on text inputs and record the inputs to all changed weight matrices, which are identified directly by comparing W W and W ′ W^{\prime} . Text-encoder matrices are probed from the prompt alone, whereas generative-backbone matrices are probed by pairing the prompt with a single fixed latent at several noise levels. Both probes require only the available model weights and architecture. The sampling loop is never executed, no image is decoded, and no model output is observed. What the attack recovers. The goal of the attack is to recover the identities of the erased concepts: a subset S ^ ⊆ 𝒞 \hat{S}\subseteq\mathcal{C} that should coincide with S ⋆ S^{\star} , together with an inferred count n n intended to match | S ⋆ | |S^{\star}| . Because Tracer automatically searches all available aligned model matrices for weight changes and reads the representations they receive, it requires no knowledge of either the erasure algorithm or its edit locations.
